transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Lee. Um... well, I guess what brings me in is that I'm having this huge issue at work. I work at a meat processing plant, and I keep starting my tasks—like the sanitation steps, the batch logs, or the end-of-line paperwork—and I just... I somehow leave out the last parts of them. 

Which is really frustrating because the paperwork is so specific. They actually just changed all our clipboards to these heavy metal ones because someone dropped a plastic one near the grinder area last year. I wasn't there when it happened, but my friend Sarah said it was a total disaster and they had to shut down the line for like three hours. Sarah just got a promotion to floor manager, actually, which is cool for her, we went to the same college so it's nice to see her moving up... 

Wait, sorry, what was I saying? Right, the paperwork. Yeah, I know my job completely depends on finishing those logs and sanitation steps correctly—like, it's a massive food safety thing—but I just keep missing the ends of them anyway.
Have you noticed this kind of difficulty finishing tasks and getting sidetracked since you were a child, or is this something that started more recently, like in the past year or so?

Um... oh, definitely since I was a kid. It's definitely not new. My mom actually still has a bunch of my old elementary school report cards in this big plastic tub in her basement. She keeps everything, honestly, like every drawing I ever made. But anyway, the ones from around fourth grade all say pretty much the same thing—that I was bright, but I needed constant reminders to actually finish my classwork and turn in my homework. 

Fourth grade was when we had Mr. Peterson. He had this really loud laugh that you could hear all the way down the hall, and he kept a pet iguana in the classroom. I loved feeding it, but I think the iguana hated me because it bit my finger once. It didn't break the skin, but it was super startling. I think that's why I prefer dogs now. My roommate just adopted a golden retriever mix, and he's the sweetest thing, though he sheds everywhere... 

But yeah, I remember I would understand the lessons perfectly fine, but I'd always miss chunks of the instructions unless Mr. Peterson was literally standing right next to me, keeping me on track. So, yeah, it's been happening for a really long time.

latest_inference.note: Childhood-onset inattention (documented on grade-school report cards), long-standing difficulty completing tasks unless externally cued, and tangential/distractible speech pattern strongly support ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. This lifelong course rules out an acquired organic cognitive disorder (F06.7). No anxiety symptoms (worry, physiological arousal) or perfectionistic/rigid personality traits are described, ruling out F41.1 and F60.5.
